digest.title: Material Intelligence — October 26, 2026
digest.description: An entirely AI-generated weekly digest of AI for materials science, based only on the supplied records.
digest.overview: This week's eight selections connect machine learning to battery interfaces, crystal screening, microstructure generation and materials characterization. The featured study pairs atomistic predictions with coating experiments; two other studies scrutinize crystal novelty and interatomic-potential benchmarks. All selected sources are preprints available here only as abstracts, not peer-reviewed findings.

stories.title: Battery coatings expose the trade-off between moisture protection and ion transport
stories.summary: Researchers combined a fine-tuned PET-MAD interatomic potential with experiments to study molecular coatings on the sulfide electrolyte Li6PS5Cl. Simulations predict that long-chain lithiated carboxylates form hydrophobic layers, with protection emerging near 0.8 nm thickness. Experiments found stronger suppression of hydrogen sulfide evolution with longer chains, while impedance measurements showed lithiated coatings retained 40–55% of initial ionic conductivity after powder processing.
stories.whyItMatters: The combination connects molecular adsorption and coating morphology to measurable protection and conductivity. Intermediate chain lengths emerge as a practical design direction because thicker barriers can exclude water while also obstructing lithium-ion transport.
stories.limitation: This abstract-only preprint does not establish long-term cycling performance or full-cell durability. The approximately 0.8 nm protection threshold is a simulation result; the experimental trends support the proposed mechanism without independently verifying every predicted structural detail.

sources.title: Combining Simulations and Spectroscopy to Design Protective Coatings on Sulfide Solid Electrolytes
sources.evidence: Sulfide solid electrolytes are attractive for all-solid-state batteries because of their high Li-ion conductivity and favorable processability, but their practical use is limited by electrochemical instability and moisture-induced degradation. Molecular surface coatings offer a scalable strategy to improve humidity tolerance and interfacial stability, yet there is limited understanding of the molecular-level factors governing surface interactions. By combining large-scale atomistic simulations enabled by a machine-learning potential with targeted experiments, we present a comprehensive framework for designing molecular coatings on Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (LPSCl). Using a PET-MAD interatomic potential fine-tuned on an r$^2$SCAN reference dataset covering LPSCl surfaces, molecular adsorbates, and their interactions, we model surface adsorption of carboxylic (CA), sulfonic (SA), and phosphonic (PA) acids with alkyl chains of varying lengths and the interaction of these coated surfaces with water at finite temperature. The simulations show that lithiated head groups generally exhibit more favorable adsorption energies. Impedance spectroscopy shows that the lithiated coatings maintain 40--55\% of the initial ionic conductivity after powder processing. While adsorption strength is largely controlled by head-group chemistry and lithiation state, coating morphology depends primarily on alkyl-chain length and surface coverage. In particular, long-chain lithiated carboxylates form dense, brush-like hydrophobic layers that reduce water access to reactive Li surface sites, with protection setting in at a coating thickness of approximately 0.8 nm. Consistent with these predictions, longer carboxylate chains suppress H$_2$S evolution more effectively. Because thicker coatings also hinder Li-ion transport, intermediate chain lengths offer the best balance between moisture protection and ionic conductivity.

stories.title: A consolidated crystal database challenges claims of generative novelty
stories.summary: A preprint reports structure-based integration of 55 databases into a collection of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values. Only 4.5% of crystal-property pairs have recorded values. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator produced 100 stiff hits versus 55 from screening, but every generated hit contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions.
stories.whyItMatters: Incomplete property coverage can make known crystals look exhausted as a discovery resource. Structural deduplication and source-traced records could improve both forward screening and the reference used to assess whether generated candidates are genuinely new.
stories.limitation: Only the preprint abstract is supplied. Repeated compositions are not necessarily duplicate structures, and the generator comparison concerns one stiffness task. Predicted stiff candidates are not experimental discoveries; the cited 428 GPa measurement for ReN2 comes from a retrospective audit of existing synthesis evidence.

sources.title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
sources.evidence: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

stories.title: Alloy-potential rankings depend on the quality of their DFT controls
stories.summary: Researchers benchmarked 14 universal machine-learned interatomic potentials against 1.45 million ordered intermetallic structures from AFLOW, which the authors report none of the models trained on. Comparisons among AFLOW, Alexandria and OQMD revealed substantial reference disagreement. After re-referencing, the best model agreed with AFLOW about as closely as Alexandria did, while the next four were 2–7 meV per atom above that disagreement floor.
stories.whyItMatters: Benchmark error can mix model shortcomings with inconsistent reference calculations. Explicit database controls and elemental-reference checks could prevent misleading rankings and help identify which apparent failures merit new calculations rather than model retraining.
stories.limitation: This abstract-only preprint primarily addresses ordered intermetallic energy and stability comparisons. Agreement within cross-database variation does not establish experimental accuracy or reliable behavior for defects, finite-temperature dynamics and other configurations outside the benchmark.

sources.title: How good are universal MLIPs for alloys? A benchmark is only as trustworthy as its controls
sources.evidence: Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are ranked by their formation-energy error against a DFT database, as if that database were ground truth, but independent DFT databases disagree. We benchmark fourteen uMLIPs on 1.45 million ordered intermetallics against AFLOW, which none trained on, and compare every energy and stability error with that disagreement. For half the structures, AFLOW, Alexandria, and OQMD differ by less than 6-8 meV/atom, but a minority differ by far more, raising the average to 16-30. That disagreement sets a floor on any model's measurable error. Re-referenced, the best uMLIP agrees with AFLOW as closely as Alexandria does, and the next four sit 2-7 meV/atom above the floor. Once broken elemental references are screened, the energy and stability rankings agree almost everywhere. Three apparent model failures shrink or vanish under the right control: poorly correlated shear moduli, thousands of "bad" DFT references, and the leader's inflated lead.

stories.title: ML-assisted screening maps ordering and distortion in sodium cathodes
stories.summary: Using a library of 41 sodium/vacancy orderings, researchers screened more than 120,000 layered-oxide structures with machine-learning interatomic potentials before performing 1,025 first-principles calculations. The resulting phase diagrams explain reported stacking sequences and voltages. Their analysis favors combining high-voltage redox chemistry with low Jahn–Teller strain and identifies Na_xMn0.5Ni0.5O2 as a practical composition within the study.
stories.whyItMatters: The workflow connects composition, charge transfer and cooperative distortion rather than relying on a single structural descriptor. It also reports release of an ordering-resolved dataset that could support more accurate potentials for related sodium-ion electrode searches.
stories.limitation: The supplied evidence is a preprint abstract describing computational results, not new battery testing. The search applies a fixed ordering library to selected transition metals, and key stacking competitions involve only a few meV per atom, making small energy differences consequential.

sources.title: Decoding Composition-Structure-Performance Relations in Sodium Layered Oxide Positive Electrode Materials
sources.evidence: Layered sodium transition-metal (TM) oxides, Na$_x$TMO$_2$, are among the most promising sodium-ion positive electrode materials, yet their Na/vacancy orderings, layer stacking sequences, and cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions are known only for a few single-TM compounds. We compile the Na/vacancy orderings reported in earlier studies into a single library of 41 unique orderings and apply this uniformly to five single-TM and all ten Na$_x$TM$_{0.5}$TM$'_{0.5}$O$_2$ oxides (TM = Ti, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni), screening more than 120,000 structures with machine-learning interatomic potentials prior to 1,025 accurate first-principles calculations. The phase diagrams explain the observed O3/P3/O1 sequences and voltages, and the O3-to-P3 competition hinges on ordering energies of a few meV per atom that scalar descriptors, such as the cationic potential and the interlayer-slab distance, miss. Our extensive analysis reveals that the redox couples form a nearly partner-independent ladder, Ti$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Mn$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Co$^{3+/4+}$ $<$ Ni$^{2+/3+}$ $<$ Fe$^{3+/4+}$, explaining pristine charge transfer and the oxidation sequence. Van Vleck analysis of every TMO$_6$ octahedron reveals that TM mixing suppresses the cooperative Jahn--Teller distortions of Mn$^{3+}$ and Ni$^{3+}$ through charge transfer to Jahn--Teller-inactive states or dilution of Jahn--Teller-active centers. We formulate an energy-density-versus-strain map that yields a design rule: a high-voltage couple without Jahn--Teller strain, which Mn$^{4+}$/Ni$^{2+}$ charge transfer realizes in Na$_x$Mn$_{0.5}$Ni$_{0.5}$O$_2$, the most practical composition. We release the ordering-resolved dataset as a training set for subsequent training of accurate machine-learning interatomic potentials.

stories.title: Symmetry-guided fine-tuning reduces the cost of thermal-conductivity calculations
stories.summary: A low-rank adaptation strategy fine-tunes MatterSim 1M on a small selection of compounds sharing a crystal symmetry, then applies the potential to other compounds with that symmetry. Across half-Heuslers, space-group-225 materials and spinels, the authors report thermal-conductivity relative errors 2–3 times smaller than with the untuned model. For 100 compounds, the reported computational time was about 5–7 times lower than individual compound fine-tuning.
stories.whyItMatters: Sharing adaptation across a structural family could make thermal-transport screening more affordable without requiring a separate fine-tuning workflow for every material. That would be useful when comparing thermoelectrics or heat-management materials within related crystal classes.
stories.limitation: This abstract-only preprint compares conductivity calculations with references obtained using moment tensor potentials and polyMLPs, not direct experimental measurements. The reported accuracy and speed gains apply to the tested families and do not establish transfer across arbitrary symmetries or chemistries.

sources.title: Symmetry-Based Parameter Efficient Low-Rank Fine-Tuning for High-Throughput Calculation of Lattice Thermal Conductivity
sources.evidence: Accurate and efficient prediction of lattice thermal conductivity (LTC) is essential for developing materials for thermoelectric, microelectronic, and photovoltaic applications. Here, we present a methodology for high-throughput calculation of LTC across large datasets of compounds sharing a common crystal symmetry. Our approach combines fine-tuning of the MatterSim 1M universal machine-learned interatomic potential with LTC calculations based on the solution of the Boltzmann transport equation. We introduce a symmetry-based few-shot fine-tuning strategy (SBFS-FT) based on low-rank adaptation. In this approach, MatterSim 1M is fine-tuned on a small, carefully selected set of compounds that share a common crystal symmetry. The resulting potential is then applicable for accurate LTC calculations for compounds with this crystal symmetry, even if they were not included in the fine-tuning set. We tested our methodology on datasets of half-Heusler compounds (space group 216), materials with space group 225, and spinels (space group 227). We demonstrated that LTC calculations with MatterSim 1M fine-tuned using SBFS-FT exhibited a mean absolute relative difference from the reference results (obtained using moment tensor potentials and polyMLPs) 2-3 times smaller than that achieved with the non-fine-tuned MatterSim 1M potential. Moreover, the accuracy of LTC calculations with MatterSim 1M after SBFS-FT was comparable to that achieved using the MatterSim 1M potentials individually fine-tuned for each compound. Importantly, SBFS-FT enabled generation of the potential suitable for accurate LTC calculations across large compound datasets substantially faster than fine-tuning of MatterSim 1M for each compound individually, reducing the computational time by approximately a factor of 5-7 for a dataset of 100 compounds.

stories.title: Diffusion models generate microstructure inputs for additive-manufacturing digital twins
stories.summary: Researchers report denoising diffusion models that synthesize orientation-imaging micrographs containing morphological and crystallographic features of metal additive-manufacturing microstructures. They also introduce classifier-free guidance for property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse mappings, with an example aimed at qualification-related uncertainty quantification.
stories.whyItMatters: Realistic synthetic microstructures could expand the inputs available to crystal-plasticity simulations when measured datasets are scarce. Conditional generation could help explore structural variability associated with a target property or processing condition.
stories.limitation: The preprint abstract reports quantitative fidelity assessment but provides no numerical metrics. Realistic generated images do not by themselves establish accurate mechanical properties, physically achievable processing routes or qualification-ready uncertainty estimates.

sources.title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
sources.evidence: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

stories.title: Composable neural inference combines X-ray and neutron reflectometry
stories.summary: A probabilistic framework trains posterior estimators separately for individual scattering measurements, then combines them at inference time using a compositional sampler. Reflectometry demonstrations cover X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron observations, including co-refinement across neutron contrasts and across X-ray and neutron measurements.
stories.whyItMatters: Combining complementary probes can reduce structural ambiguity in thin films and interfaces. Reusing individual estimators without dedicated joint retraining could make uncertainty-aware analysis more modular as measurement combinations change.
stories.limitation: This abstract-only preprint demonstrates reflectometry applications, not general resolution of scattering inverse problems. The supplied evidence does not quantify uncertainty calibration, runtime or robustness to inconsistent measurements; broader scattering applications remain prospective.

sources.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
sources.evidence: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

stories.title: ML potentials disentangle thermal expansion from heat transport in anharmonic crystals
stories.summary: Actively learned moment tensor potentials enabled molecular-dynamics studies of Rb2SO4, Rb2Ca2(SO4)3 and Ba3Lu(BO3)3. Simulations reproduced measured thermal expansion and supported previously proposed structural mechanisms. Calculated thermal conductivities differed by more than an order of magnitude between compounds with comparable anharmonicity measures, while predicted temperature-driven band-gap renormalization reached 2.7 eV in one compound.
stories.whyItMatters: The results illustrate how ML-enabled dynamics can connect atomic rearrangements to thermal and electronic properties in systems poorly described by harmonic models. They also caution against using a single anharmonicity metric as a shortcut for predicting heat transport.
stories.limitation: The evidence is limited to a preprint abstract. Thermal-expansion agreement provides an experimental check, but the conductivity and band-gap changes are computational predictions in the supplied record. Their accuracy depends on the underlying density-functional data and learned potentials.

sources.title: Thermal expansion mechanisms, heat transport, and band-gap renormalization in strongly anharmonic Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ from machine-learned interatomic potentials
sources.evidence: Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ are structurally complex materials whose thermal expansion has been interpreted, on the basis of high-temperature x-ray diffraction, in terms of specific polyhedral rearrangements. We study their lattice dynamics and its consequences for thermal and electronic properties using molecular dynamics with actively learned moment tensor potentials trained on density-functional theory data. The anharmonicity measure $σ^A$ (compares the anharmonic contribution to the interatomic forces with the total forces acting on atoms) reaches $\approx$0.3-0.5 for $β$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ and $\approx$0.75 for orientationally disordered $α$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, and the imaginary harmonic modes of Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and $α$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$ are stabilized at finite temperature. The simulations reproduce the measured thermal expansion and support the mechanisms proposed from diffraction: expansion along $c$ in $β$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$ arises from both elongation and straightening of corrugated Rb chains, BO$_3$ reorientation accompanies the anisotropic expansion of Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$, and bending of polyhedral linkages limits expansion along the weakly expanding directions and in cubic Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$. Green-Kubo lattice thermal conductivities differ by more than an order of magnitude between compounds with comparable $σ^A$, showing that the anharmonicity measure alone does not determine heat transport. Phonon-induced band-gap renormalization, including lattice thermal expansion, reaches 2.7 and 1.7 eV at 1250 K in Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$ and 1.4 eV at 650 K in $β$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, with zero-point renormalizations of 0.64, 0.70, and 0.31 eV for $β$-Rb$_2$SO$_4$, Rb$_2$Ca$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, and Ba$_3$Lu(BO$_3$)$_3$, respectively.
